claim: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) acetate, propionate, and butyrate are produced in large quantities by the gut microbiome.
source: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) acetate, propionate, and butyrate are produced in large quantities by the gut microbiome and contribute to a wide array of physiological processes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about SCFA production.

claim: SCFAs contribute to a wide array of physiological processes.
source: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) acetate, propionate, and butyrate are produced in large quantities by the gut microbiome and contribute to a wide array of physiological processes.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Many effects of SCFAs have been traced to changes in the cell's epigenetic state.
source: While the underlying mechanisms are largely unknown, many effects of SCFAs have been traced to changes in the cell's epigenetic state.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Butyrate and propionate induce rapid and sustained increases in histone acetylation.
source: Using quantitative proteomics of histone modification states, we identified rapid and sustained increases in histone acetylation after the addition of butyrate or propionate, but not acetate.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's quantitative proteomics experiments.

claim: Acetate does not induce rapid and sustained increases in histone acetylation.
source: Using quantitative proteomics of histone modification states, we identified rapid and sustained increases in histone acetylation after the addition of butyrate or propionate, but not acetate.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's quantitative proteomics experiments.

claim: Propionate and butyrate activate the acetyltransferase p300 rather than inhibiting HDACs.
source: While decades of prior observations would suggest that hyperacetylation induced by SCFAs are due to inhibition of histone deacetylases (HDACs), we found that propionate and butyrate instead activate the acetyltransferase p300.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Propionate and butyrate are rapidly converted to the corresponding acyl-CoAs.
source: Propionate and butyrate are rapidly converted to the corresponding acyl-CoAs which are then used by p300 to catalyze auto-acylation of the autoinhibitory loop, activating the enzyme for histone/protein acetylation.
evidence: This is a key mechanistic finding from metabolomics experiments.

claim: Acyl-CoAs are used by p300 to catalyze auto-acylation of the autoinhibitory loop.
source: Propionate and butyrate are rapidly converted to the corresponding acyl-CoAs which are then used by p300 to catalyze auto-acylation of the autoinhibitory loop, activating the enzyme for histone/protein acetylation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from biochemical assays.

claim: Auto-acylation of the autoinhibitory loop activates p300 for histone/protein acetylation.
source: Propionate and butyrate are rapidly converted to the corresponding acyl-CoAs which are then used by p300 to catalyze auto-acylation of the autoinhibitory loop, activating the enzyme for histone/protein acetylation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from biochemical assays.

claim: SCFAs include any fatty acid with fewer than six carbons.
source: Although SCFAs include any fatty acid with fewer than six carbons, the first three members of the family—acetate, propionate, and butyrate—are by far the most abundant physiologically (den Besten et al., 2013; Koh et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Acetate, propionate, and butyrate are the most abundant SCFAs physiologically.
source: Although SCFAs include any fatty acid with fewer than six carbons, the first three members of the family—acetate, propionate, and butyrate—are by far the most abundant physiologically (den Besten et al., 2013; Koh et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SCFAs are produced by bacterial fermentation of nondigestible fiber.
source: These three SCFAs are produced in large quantities by bacterial fermentation of nondigestible fiber, and levels can fluctuate based on the amount and type of fiber in the diet (Bird et al., 2000; den Besten et al., 2013; Jenkins et al., 1998; Levrat et al., 1991; Marsono et al., 1993; Ríos-Covián et al., 2016; Velázquez et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: SCFA levels can fluctuate based on the amount and type of fiber in the diet.
source: These three SCFAs are produced in large quantities by bacterial fermentation of nondigestible fiber, and levels can fluctuate based on the amount and type of fiber in the diet (Bird et al., 2000; den Besten et al., 2013; Jenkins et al., 1998; Levrat et al., 1991; Marsono et al., 1993; Ríos-Covián et al., 2016; Velázquez et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Total SCFA concentrations can reach over 100 mM in the human colon.
source: In humans, total SCFA concentrations can reach over 100 mM in the colon, in a ratio of ~60:20:20 acetate:propionate:butyrate (Cummings et al., 1987; Parada Venegas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SCFAs exist in the human colon in a ratio of approximately 60:20:20 acetate:propionate:butyrate.
source: In humans, total SCFA concentrations can reach over 100 mM in the colon, in a ratio of ~60:20:20 acetate:propionate:butyrate (Cummings et al., 1987; Parada Venegas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SCFAs may provide up to 10% of daily caloric requirements in humans.
source: SCFAs alone may provide up to 10% of daily caloric requirements in humans (Bergman, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Colonocytes derive 60–70% of their energy from SCFA oxidation.
source: Colonocytes are especially prone to metabolize SCFAs, deriving 60–70% of their energy from SCFA oxidation (Roediger, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Excess SCFAs are transported to the liver through the portal vein.
source: Excess SCFAs are transported to the liver through the portal vein and are eventually released into the peripheral blood, existing at micromolar concentrations (Bloemen et al., 2009; Cummings et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SCFAs exist at micromolar concentrations in peripheral blood.
source: Excess SCFAs are transported to the liver through the portal vein and are eventually released into the peripheral blood, existing at micromolar concentrations (Bloemen et al., 2009; Cummings et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Butyrate has been reported to improve intestinal barrier function.
source: The physiological effects of butyrate are abundant: butyrate has been reported among other things to improve intestinal barrier function (Chang et al., 2014; Hamer et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2009), reduce inflammation (Chriett et al., 2019; Usami et al., 2008; Vinolo et al., 2011), improve metabolic health (Gao et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2019), and prevent cancer (Donohoe et al., 2012; Hague et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Butyrate has been reported to reduce inflammation.
source: The physiological effects of butyrate are abundant: butyrate has been reported among other things to improve intestinal barrier function (Chang et al., 2014; Hamer et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2009), reduce inflammation (Chriett et al., 2019; Usami et al., 2008; Vinolo et al., 2011), improve metabolic health (Gao et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2019), and prevent cancer (Donohoe et al., 2012; Hague et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Butyrate has been reported to improve metabolic health.
source: The physiological effects of butyrate are abundant: butyrate has been reported among other things to improve intestinal barrier function (Chang et al., 2014; Hamer et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2009), reduce inflammation (Chriett et al., 2019; Usami et al., 2008; Vinolo et al., 2011), improve metabolic health (Gao et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2019), and prevent cancer (Donohoe et al., 2012; Hague et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Butyrate has been reported to prevent cancer.
source: The physiological effects of butyrate are abundant: butyrate has been reported among other things to improve intestinal barrier function (Chang et al., 2014; Hamer et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2009), reduce inflammation (Chriett et al., 2019; Usami et al., 2008; Vinolo et al., 2011), improve metabolic health (Gao et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2019), and prevent cancer (Donohoe et al., 2012; Hague et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Extremely high levels of propionate are associated with negative health outcomes such as propionic acidemia and autism spectrum disorders.
source: The role of propionate is less clear—while it shows the same beneficial effects as butyrate in many studies, extremely high levels of propionate are associated with negative health outcomes such as propionic acidemia and autism spectrum disorders (Abdelli et al., 2019; Al-Lahham et al., 2010; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It is generally believed that SCFAs induce physiological effects by changing the cell's epigenetic state.
source: It is generally believed that SCFAs induce physiological effects by changing the cell's epigenetic state (Hamer et al., 2007; Hinnebusch et al., 2002; Krautkramer et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Histone PTMs affect a wide array of processes, from DNA accessibility to transcription factor binding.
source: Histone PTMs affect a wide array of processes, from DNA accessibility to transcription factor binding (Bannister and Kouzarides, 2011; Karch et al., 2013; Kouzarides, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Lysine acetylation opens chromatin and makes it more accessible to transcription.
source: Histone PTMs include lysine acetylation, which opens chromatin and makes it more accessible to transcription, and lysine methylation, which performs various functions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about histone modifications.

claim: Histone PTMs are exquisitely sensitive to changes in cellular metabolism.
source: Histone PTMs, as well as the enzymes which add or remove them, are exquisitely sensitive to changes in cellular metabolism (Albaugh et al., 2011; Fan et al., 2015; Sassone-Corsi, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Acetyl-CoA is used to acetylate histones.
source: Several central metabolites are also substrates for histone modifications: such as acetyl-CoA, which is used to acetylate histones.
evidence: This is established knowledge about histone acetylation.

claim: Histone acetylation is regulated by histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and histone deacetylases (HDACs).
source: Histone acetylation is regulated on two fronts—first by histone acetyltransferases (HATs), which transfer acetyl groups to chromatin, and then by histone deacetylases (HDACs), which remove them (Albaugh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Acetate, propionate, and butyrate have all been reported to inhibit HDACs to varying extents, with butyrate being the most potent inhibitor.
source: Acetate, propionate, and butyrate have all been reported to inhibit HDACs to varying extents, with butyrate being the most potent inhibitor (Bolduc et al., 2017; Candido et al., 1978; Davie, 2003; Hsu et al., 2016; Silva et al., 2018; Waldecker et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: HDAC inhibition has been proposed as a mechanism for SCFA's anti-cancer effects.
source: HDAC inhibition has been proposed as a mechanism for SCFA's anti-cancer effects (Donohoe et al., 2014; Hinnebusch et al., 2002), insulin regulation (Chriett et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2009), and immunomodulation (Bolduc et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2014; Usami et al., 2008; Vinolo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HDAC inhibition has been proposed as a mechanism for SCFA's insulin regulation.
source: HDAC inhibition has been proposed as a mechanism for SCFA's anti-cancer effects (Donohoe et al., 2014; Hinnebusch et al., 2002), insulin regulation (Chriett et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2009), and immunomodulation (Bolduc et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2014; Usami et al., 2008; Vinolo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HDAC inhibition has been proposed as a mechanism for SCFA's immunomodulation.
source: HDAC inhibition has been proposed as a mechanism for SCFA's anti-cancer effects (Donohoe et al., 2014; Hinnebusch et al., 2002), insulin regulation (Chriett et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2009), and immunomodulation (Bolduc et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2014; Usami et al., 2008; Vinolo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The gut microbiome can affect histone modifications systemically.
source: It has been recently reported that the gut microbiome can affect histone modifications systemically (Krautkramer et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2014; Romano et al., 2017; Takahashi et al., 2006; Wellen et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Germ-free mice display distinct patterns of histone PTMs in multiple tissues.
source: Our lab has demonstrated that germ-free mice display distinct patterns of histone PTMs in multiple tissues (Krautkramer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work from the authors' lab.

claim: Germ-free mice show decreased histone acetylation on multiple sites.
source: This phenotype was complex, but could be generally characterized by decreased histone acetylation on multiple sites.
evidence: This is a finding from prior work by the authors' lab.

claim: Supplementing germ-free mice with SCFAs in drinking water led to changes in gene expression and histone PTMs that mimicked bacterial colonization.
source: Finally, simply supplementing germ-free mice with SCFAs in drinking water led to changes in gene expression and histone PTMs that mimicked bacterial colonization.
evidence: This is a finding from prior work by the authors' lab.

claim: SCFAs are a critical link between the microbiome and epigenetic state.
source: This data strongly suggests that SCFAs are a critical link between the microbiome and epigenetic state.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work from the authors' lab.

claim: Propionate and butyrate did not affect histone methylation.
source: Propionate and butyrate induced rapid and dose-dependent increases in histone acetylation but did not affect histone methylation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the histone proteomics experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Acetate had no significant effect on histone PTMs at any dose or time point tested.
source: In contrast, acetate had no significant effect on histone PTMs at any dose or time point tested.
evidence: This is a finding from the histone proteomics experiments.

claim: The hyperacetylation phenotype with propionate and butyrate was rapid and stable, persisting for at least 24 hr.
source: The hyperacetylation phenotype with propionate and butyrate was rapid and stable, persisting for at least 24 hr (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the time course experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Changes in histone propionylation and butyrylation were detected on multiple sites, including significant increases in K18/K23 propionylation after both propionate and butyrate treatment.
source: We also detected changes in both histone propionylation and butyrylation on multiple sites, including significant increases in K18/K23 propionylation after both propionate and butyrate treatment.
evidence: This is a finding from the histone proteomics experiments.

claim: Changes in histone propionylation and butyrylation were less consistent across experiments compared to changes in histone acetylation.
source: In general, changes in histone propionylation and butyrylation were less consistent across experiments compared to the robust changes in histone acetylation, likely due in part to the technical challenges of measuring low-abundance propionylation/butyrylation.
evidence: This is an observation from the histone proteomics experiments with an inference about the cause.

claim: 1 mM SCFA treatment for 1 hr did not affect media pH, media glucose, or cell viability for at least 24 hr.
source: This dose did not affect media pH, media glucose, or cell viability for at least 24 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 1 mM dose is within the physiological concentrations in the colon (which range from 0.5 to 15 mM).
source: The 1 mM dose is within the physiological concentrations in the colon (which range from 0.5 to 15 mM), but is higher than reported concentrations in other parts of the body (which range from 0 to 150 µM) (Cummings et al., 1987; Parada Venegas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The 1 mM dose is higher than reported concentrations in other parts of the body (which range from 0 to 150 µM).
source: The 1 mM dose is within the physiological concentrations in the colon (which range from 0.5 to 15 mM), but is higher than reported concentrations in other parts of the body (which range from 0 to 150 µM) (Cummings et al., 1987; Parada Venegas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HEK293, HepG2, and MCF7 cells showed remarkably similar hyperacetylation phenotypes after propionate and butyrate treatment.
source: HEK293, HepG2, and MCF7 cells showed remarkably similar hyperacetylation phenotypes after propionate and butyrate treatment (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments in multiple cell lines shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The ability of propionate and butyrate to increase histone acetylation, but not methylation, can be generalized to multiple cell types.
source: Thus, the ability of propionate and butyrate to increase histone acetylation, but not methylation, can be generalized to multiple cell types.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data from multiple cell lines.

claim: The IC50 of propionate for HDAC inhibition in HCT116 nuclear extract is 223 ± 64 µM.
source: Table 1 lists the IC50 values of HDAC inhibition for propionate, butyrate, and corresponding acyl-CoAs.
evidence: This is a finding from HDAC inhibition assays shown in Table 1.

claim: The IC50 of butyrate for HDAC inhibition in HCT116 nuclear extract is 52 ± 11 µM.
source: Table 1 lists the IC50 values of HDAC inhibition for propionate, butyrate, and corresponding acyl-CoAs.
evidence: This is a finding from HDAC inhibition assays shown in Table 1.

claim: The IC50 of propionyl-CoA for HDAC inhibition is 18 ± 7 mM.
source: Table 1 lists the IC50 values of HDAC inhibition for propionate, butyrate, and corresponding acyl-CoAs.
evidence: This is a finding from HDAC inhibition assays shown in Table 1.

claim: The IC50 of butyryl-CoA for HDAC inhibition is 1.13 ± 0.01 mM.
source: Table 1 lists the IC50 values of HDAC inhibition for propionate, butyrate, and corresponding acyl-CoAs.
evidence: This is a finding from HDAC inhibition assays shown in Table 1.

claim: The determined IC50 values are on the low end of previously published values, which range from 50 to 300 µM in nuclear extract and 1–10 mM in whole cells.
source: These IC50 values are on the low end of previously published values, which range from 50 to 300 µM in nuclear extract and 1–10 mM in whole cells (Huber et al., 2011; Silva et al., 2018; Vinolo et al., 2011; Waldecker et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature supported by citations.

claim: Intracellular concentrations of SCFAs are much lower than extracellular concentrations.
source: While SCFA concentrations in media were theoretically higher than our determined IC50 values (Figure 2C), it has been previously reported that intracellular concentrations of SCFAs are much lower than extracellular concentrations, which could have bearing on this mechanism (Donohoe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SCFA concentrations in media declined from 1 mM to 0.5 mM over 24 hr.
source: After treatments, SCFA concentrations in media declined from 1 mM to 0.5 mM over 24 hr.
evidence: This is a finding from metabolomics experiments.

claim: SCFA levels measured in cellular extractions were similar among the three SCFAs (max ~3-fold difference), with all showing a decline by 24 hr.
source: SCFA levels measured in cellular extractions were similar among the three SCFAs (max ~3-fold difference), with all showing a decline by 24 hr (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from metabolomics experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Intracellular concentrations of butyrate are estimated at ~40 µM.
source: From levels determined in the cellular extractions, we estimated intracellular concentrations of ~40 µM for butyrate and ~100 µM for propionate and acetate, which are consistent with previous reports (Donohoe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an estimate based on metabolomics data, consistent with prior literature.

claim: Intracellular concentrations of propionate and acetate are estimated at ~100 µM.
source: From levels determined in the cellular extractions, we estimated intracellular concentrations of ~40 µM for butyrate and ~100 µM for propionate and acetate, which are consistent with previous reports (Donohoe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an estimate based on metabolomics data, consistent with prior literature.

claim: The bulk of the decrease in media SCFA concentration was due to volatility and not to cellular consumption.
source: In additional control experiments, SCFA concentrations in media without cells incubated at 37°C declined at almost an identical rate as that observed in media incubated with cells, suggesting that the bulk of the decrease in media SCFA concentration was due to volatility and not to cellular consumption (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Free SCFAs are rapidly metabolized instead of building up in cells.
source: The calculated values suggest that free SCFAs are rapidly metabolized instead of building up in cells (Boets et al., 2017; Clausen and Mortensen, 1994; Clausen and Mortensen, 1995).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: No significant labeling of TCA cycle metabolites was found after propionate and butyrate treatment.
source: However, we found no significant labeling of TCA cycle metabolites after propionate and butyrate treatment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from metabolomics experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Labeled carbons built up as acyl-carnitine species, appearing in as little as 10 min and remaining stable for 24 hrs.
source: Instead, labeled carbons built up as acyl-carnitine species, appearing in as little as 10 min and remaining stable for 24 hrs (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from metabolomics experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Acyl-carnitine buildup did not occur in acetate-treated cells.
source: Intriguingly, this buildup did not occur in acetate-treated cells.
evidence: This is a finding from metabolomics experiments.

claim: Accumulation of acyl-CoAs after SCFA treatment has been previously reported.
source: Accumulation of acyl-CoAs after SCFA treatment has been previously reported (Basu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Free carnitine and free CoA levels did not significantly change under the experimental conditions.
source: Under our conditions, however, free carnitine and free CoA levels did not significantly change (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from metabolomics experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: All cell lines showed the same upregulation of acyl-carnitines after butyrate and propionate treatment.
source: All cell lines showed the same upregulation of acyl-carnitines after butyrate and propionate treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from metabolomics experiments in multiple cell lines shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Histone hyperacetylation may be due to the presence of propionyl- or butyryl-CoA rather than intracellular propionate or butyrate.
source: Ultimately, these data suggest that histone hyperacetylation may not be due to the presence of intracellular propionate or butyrate, as the intracellular levels of these metabolites are low, but to the presence of propionyl- or butyryl-CoA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolomics data.

claim: Propionyl- and butyryl-CoA do not inhibit HDAC at physiological concentrations.
source: Since propionyl- and butyryl-CoA do not inhibit HDAC at physiological concentrations, this raises the possibility that the histone hyperacetylation phenotype may not be due to HDAC inhibition, but to a different mechanism (Table 1; Vogelauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the IC50 values in Table 1 and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Treatment with 13C-labeled SCFAs for 4 hr resulted in only 1–5% 13C-labeling on histones.
source: To test whether this occurred in our system, we performed histone proteomics after a 4-hr treatment with 13C-labeled SCFAs. This treatment only resulted in 1–5% 13C-labeling on histones, which cannot account for the two- or threefold increases in histone acetylation seen after SCFA treatment (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from isotope labeling experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The majority of new acetyl groups (~90–95%) were not generated from labeled SCFAs.
source: This indicates that the majority of new acetyl groups (~90–95%) were not generated from labeled SCFAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the isotope labeling data.

claim: siRNA knockdown or genetic knockout of ACLY, ACSS2, and PCC had no significant effect on propionate or butyrate-induced histone acetylation.
source: siRNA knockdown or genetic knockout of ACLY (an enzyme involved in transport of acetyl-CoA out of the mitochondria), ACSS2 (the cytoplasmic acetyl-CoA ligase), and PCC (an enzyme in the pathway that metabolizes propionyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA) had no significant effect on propionate or butyrate-induced histone acetylation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Acyl-CoAs are not metabolized to acetyl-CoA in sufficient quantities to explain the induced hyperacetylation.
source: This data indicates that acyl-CoAs are not metabolized to acetyl-CoA in sufficient quantities to explain the induced hyperacetylation, indicating a different mechanism is at play.
evidence: This is an inference based on the knockdown experiments and isotope labeling data.

claim: Propionyl- and butyryl-CoA induced dose-dependent increases in the HAT activity of nuclear extract.
source: HAT assays demonstrated that propionyl- and butyryl-CoA induced dose-dependent increases in the HAT activity of nuclear extract (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from HAT activity assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Free propionate and butyrate had no effect on HAT activity.
source: Free propionate and butyrate had no effect.
evidence: This is a finding from HAT activity assays.

claim: p300/CBP acetylates a large number of lysine sites in vitro.
source: However, p300/CBP acetylates a large number of lysine sites in vitro, and is known to target several of our measured hyperacetylation sites in vivo (Henry et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: p300/CBP encode an autoinhibitory loop (AIL) which must be auto-acetylated to stimulate HAT activity.
source: Both proteins encode an autoinhibitory loop (AIL, also called the autoregulatory or activation loop), which must be auto-acetylated to stimulate HAT activity (Karanam et al., 2006; Thompson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Large-scale mass-spectrometry surveys have identified sites of propionylation and butyrylation on p300, including on several AIL lysines.
source: Large-scale mass-spectrometry surveys have identified sites of propionylation and butyrylation on p300, including on several AIL lysines; however, how these modifications are added and whether they have a functional consequence on p300 activity are not known (Chen et al., 2007; Cheng et al., 2009; Kaczmarska et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recombinant p300 performed auto-acylation with propionyl- or butyryl-CoA at rates indistinguishable from auto-acetylation with acetyl-CoA.
source: Indeed, we found that recombinant p300 performed auto-acylation with propionyl- or butyryl-CoA at rates indistinguishable from auto-acetylation with acetyl-CoA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from biochemical assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Auto-acylation was catalytic, as heat-denatured p300 did not show increases in acylation under the same conditions.
source: Auto-acylation was catalytic, as heat-denatured p300 did not show increases in acylation under the same conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Proteomics analysis confirmed the location of propionylation and butyrylation on several AIL lysine sites.
source: Proteomics analysis confirmed the location of propionylation and butyrylation on several AIL lysine sites under these conditions (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from proteomics analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: All forms of acylated p300 (acetylated, propionylated, and butyrylated) were significantly more active than an unmodified control.
source: All forms of acylated p300 (acetylated, propionylated, and butyrylated) were significantly more active than an unmodified control (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from radioactive HAT assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There were no significant differences in the activity of auto-acetylated, propionylated, or butyrylated p300, which all showed ~500% increase in their initial rates compared to unmodified p300.
source: In addition, there were no significant differences in the activity of auto-acetylated, propionylated, or butyrylated p300, which all showed ~500% increase in their initial rates compared to unmodified p300.
evidence: This is a finding from radioactive HAT assays.

claim: p300 catalyzes auto-butyrylation and propionylation on AIL sites, and auto-acylation activates the enzyme in a similar manner to auto-acetylation.
source: In all, these data demonstrate that p300 catalyzes auto-butyrylation and propionylation on AIL sites, and that auto-acylation activates the enzyme in a similar manner to auto-acetylation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple biochemical assays.

claim: A485 treatment reversed SCFA-induced hyperacetylation on p300 targets H3K27 and H3K18.
source: Indeed, A485 treatment reversed SCFA-induced hyperacetylation on p300 targets H3K27 and H3K18 (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A485 treatment reversed SCFA-induced hyperacetylation on the non-histone p300 substrate p53 (K382).
source: A485 treatment did not just reverse SCFA-induced hyperacetylation on histone substrates of p300, but also on the non-histone p300 substrate p53 (K382).
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological inhibition experiments.

claim: Treatment with 10 µM SAHA should effectively saturate HDAC inhibition, at least of class I and II HDACs.
source: Treatment with 10 µM of this potent pan-HDAC inhibitor should effectively saturate HDAC inhibition, at least of class I and II HDACs, which are known to target these sites (Caslini et al., 2019; Kelly et al., 2018; Rajan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known IC50 of SAHA and citations to prior literature.

claim: 100 µM treatment of propionate or butyrate with SAHA still led to significant increases in p53K382 acetylation over a SAHA control.
source: However, 100 µM treatment of propionate or butyrate with SAHA still led to significant increases in p53K382 acetylation over a SAHA control (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from pharmacological inhibition experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Propionate and butyrate induce histone hyperacetylation by an alternative mechanism to HDAC inhibition, likely through the auto-activation of p300 by rapidly formed acyl-CoAs.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that propionate and butyrate induce histone hyperacetylation by an alternative mechanism to HDAC inhibition, likely through the auto-activation of p300 by rapidly formed acyl-CoAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pharmacological inhibition experiments.

claim: 500 µM propionate treatment induced significant increases in histone acetylation after sham and WT transfections.
source: As expected, 500 µM propionate treatment induced significant increases in histone acetylation after sham and WT transfections (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: This is a finding from transfection experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cells transfected with the ΔGlu mutant showed significantly smaller increases in acetylation, approximately half of that seen in WT-transfected cells.
source: However, cells transfected with the ΔGlu mutant showed significantly smaller increases in acetylation, approximately half of that seen in WT-transfected cells.
evidence: This is a finding from transfection experiments.

claim: The AIL lysines of p300 are necessary to induce the full extent of histone hyperacetylation after propionate treatment.
source: Nevertheless, these data strongly suggest that the AIL lysines of p300 are necessary to induce the full extent of histone hyperacetylation after propionate treatment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transfection experiments with the ΔGlu mutant.

claim: p300 immunoprecipitated from propionate and butyrate-treated cells showed small but significant increases in activity in a radioactive HAT assay.
source: p300 immunoprecipitated from propionate and butyrate-treated cells showed small but significant increases in activity in a radioactive HAT assay (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Western blots identified increased propionylation and butyrylation of p300 immunoprecipitated from propionate and butyrate-treated cells.
source: Corresponding western blots also identified increased propionylation and butyrylation of p300 under these conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: p300 activation, rather than HDAC inhibition, plays a critical role for propionate and butyrate-induced chromatin hyperacetylation at low concentrations.
source: In all, our results demonstrate that p300 activation, rather than HDAC inhibition, plays a critical role for propionate and butyrate-induced chromatin hyperacetylation at low concentrations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data.

claim: For decades, butyrate and propionate's ability to alter chromatin have been attributed to HDAC inhibition.
source: For decades, butyrate and propionate's ability to alter chromatin have been attributed to HDAC inhibition (Candido et al., 1978).
evidence: This is a statement about the historical understanding, supported by a citation.

claim: Reported IC50 values for butyrate and propionate range between 50 and 300 µM in nuclear extract and between 1 and 10 mM in whole cells.
source: However, the IC50 values for these two molecules are quite high, with reported values ranging between 50 and 300 µM in nuclear extract and between 1 and 10 mM in whole cells (Huber et al., 2011; Silva et al., 2018; Vinolo et al., 2011; Waldecker et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SCFAs can induce histone hyperacetylation in colon, liver, and adipose tissue, which experience SCFA concentrations that differ by orders of magnitude.
source: In addition, our previous data suggests that SCFAs can induce histone hyperacetylation in colon, liver, and adipose tissue, which experience SCFA concentrations that differ by orders of magnitude (Krautkramer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work from the authors' lab.

claim: Intracellular concentrations of SCFAs could be significantly lower than exterior concentrations.
source: Even in the gut, intracellular concentrations of SCFAs could be significantly lower than exterior concentrations (Donohoe et al., 2012; Sengupta et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Km values for p300 auto-acetylation lie in the nM to low µM range.
source: While the IC50 values for HDAC inhibition are in the high µM to mM range, Km values for p300 auto-acetylation lie in the nM to low µM range (Karanam et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hyperacetylation induced by high doses of butyrate (2–5 mM) are almost immediately reversed after butyrate withdrawal.
source: Hyperacetylation induced by high doses of butyrate (2–5 mM) are almost immediately reversed after butyrate withdrawal (Prasad and Sinha, 1976; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Auto-acetylation of p300 increases its half-life from 4.5 to >24 hr.
source: In contrast, auto-acetylation of p300 increases its half-life from 4.5 to >24 hr (Jain et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Even after extracellular SCFAs have been fully metabolized, modified p300 could still theoretically induce hyperacetylation.
source: Thus, even after extracellular SCFAs have been fully metabolized, modified p300 could still theoretically induce hyperacetylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known half-life of auto-acetylated p300.

claim: Auto-acylation of p300 may prove a primary mechanism in physiological systems where SCFA concentrations are low.
source: Auto-acylation of p300 may thus prove a primary mechanism in physiological systems where SCFA concentrations are low.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Acetate treatment has been previously reported to increase histone acetylation, but only under extreme conditions such as hypoxia or after genetic manipulation.
source: Acetate treatment has been previously reported to increase histone acetylation, but only under extreme conditions such as hypoxia (Bulusu et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2016), or after genetic manipulation (Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Others have reported no effect of acetate in conditions similar to those described in this study.
source: Others have reported no effect of acetate in conditions similar to those described here (Hinnebusch et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Acetate's lack of effect can be explained by the fact that acetate is not rapidly metabolized to acetyl-CoA, as propionate and butyrate are to their respective acyl-CoAs.
source: Based on the results reported here, acetate's lack of effect can be explained by the fact that acetate is not rapidly metabolized to acetyl-CoA, as propionate and butyrate are to their respective acyl-CoAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: Under normal conditions, acetyl-CoA is mainly generated in the mitochondria from glucose.
source: Instead, under normal conditions, acetyl-CoA is mainly generated in the mitochondria from glucose (Wellen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: There is no evidence to date of acetyl-CoA crossing the mitochondrial membrane.
source: Since there is no evidence to date of acetyl-CoA crossing the mitochondrial membrane, acetyl-CoA must be shuttled to the cytosol via citrate.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Citrate is converted into oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA by ATP citrate lyase (ACLY) in the cytosol.
source: Once in the cytosol, citrate is converted into oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA by ATP citrate lyase (ACLY).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular metabolism.

claim: Stress conditions such as hypoxia, or genetic knockout of ACLY, can cause the cell to rely on acetate for acetyl-CoA production.
source: However, stress conditions such as hypoxia, or genetic knockout of ACLY, can cause the cell to rely on acetate for acetyl-CoA production (Bulusu et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: p300 auto-acylation and activation via SCFAs depend on robust cellular synthesis of the corresponding acyl-CoAs.
source: However, our results suggest that p300 auto-acylation and activation via SCFAs depend on robust cellular synthesis of the corresponding acyl-CoAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: In cells treated with mixtures of SCFAs, acetylation increased based only on the sum of butyrate and propionate concentrations.
source: However, there is some data to suggest that in cells treated with mixtures of SCFAs, acetylation increased based only on the sum of butyrate and propionate concentrations (Kiefer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The use of normal or dialyzed fetal bovine serum (FBS) in cell culture media did not affect the histone hyperacetylation phenotype.
source: This is consistent with our observation that the use of normal or dialyzed fetal bovine serum (FBS) in cell culture media did not affect the histone hyperacetylation phenotype (dialyzed FBS does not contain acetate).
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: SCFA treatment phenocopies other HDAC inhibitors in some cases but not others.
source: SCFA treatment phenocopies other HDAC inhibitors in some cases (Chang et al., 2014; Rahman et al., 2003; Zhou et al., 2011), but not others (Milton et al., 2012; Siavoshian et al., 2000; Zhao et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several groups have reported that certain phosphatase or PKC inhibitors can reverse SCFA-induced hyperacetylation.
source: In addition, several groups have reported that certain phosphatase or PKC inhibitors can reverse SCFA-induced hyperacetylation (Cuisset et al., 1997; Cuisset et al., 1998; Rickard et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Phosphatase or PKC inhibitors are known to interact with p300.
source: While it has been proposed that this is due to phosphorylation of HDACs (Davie, 2003), it is interesting to note that these inhibitors are also known to interact with p300 (H.-H. Cheng et al., 2014; Granja et al., 2008; Zgheib et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Rates of acylation decrease as acyl chains increase, to the extent that butyryl-CoA can act as a competitive inhibitor for some HATs.
source: In general, rates of acylation decrease as acyl chains increase, to the extent that butyryl-CoA can act as a competitive inhibitor for some HATs (Carrer et al., 2017; Montgomery et al., 2015; Ringel and Wolberger, 2016; Simithy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A sharp increase in acyl-CoA concentrations could slow most HATs, which cannot efficiently use longer acyl-CoAs as substrates.
source: Thus, a sharp increase in acyl-CoA concentrations could slow most HATs, which cannot efficiently use longer acyl-CoAs as substrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior literature about HAT substrate preferences.

claim: p300 is less efficient at histone propionylation and butyrylation than it is at histone acetylation.
source: Intriguingly, previous reports indicate that p300 is also less efficient at histone propionylation and butyrylation than it is at histone acetylation (Kaczmarska et al., 2017), which is consistent with our histone PTM analyses (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and is consistent with the data in Figure 1.

claim: The measured rates of p300 auto-acylation were indistinguishable between acetate, propionate, and butyrate.
source: However, our measured rates of p300 auto-acylation were indistinguishable between acetate, propionate, and butyrate.
evidence: This is a finding from the biochemical assays.

claim: The reported Km of p300 for auto-acetylation (~100 nM) is lower than for acetylation of histone substrates (~6 µM).
source: In addition, the reported Km of p300 for auto-acetylation (~100 nM) is lower than for acetylation of histone substrates (~6 µM) (Karanam et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: p300 may prefer to use acyl-CoAs to auto-acylate, which would activate the enzyme toward other substrates targeted for acetylation.
source: Thus, p300 may prefer to use acyl-CoAs to auto-acylate, which would activate the enzyme toward other substrates targeted for acetylation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings and prior literature.

claim: Higher concentrations of acyl-CoAs may slow or inhibit other HATs but could preferentially activate p300 via auto-acylation.
source: In that case, while higher concentrations of acyl-CoAs may slow or inhibit other HATs, they could preferentially activate p300 via auto-acylation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings and prior literature.

claim: The proteomics data shows more robust increases in histone acetylation than histone propionylation or butyrylation.
source: The fact that our proteomics data shows more robust increases in histone acetylation than histone propionylation or butyrylation would further support this hypothesis (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the proteomics data in Figure 1.

claim: SCFAs are known to bind and activate several G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), especially FFAR2, FFAR3, and HCAR2.
source: It should be noted that SCFAs are also known to bind and activate several G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), especially FFAR2, FFAR3, and HCAR2 (Brown et al., 2003; Inoue et al., 2014; Priyadarshini et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2014; Thangaraju et al., 2009; Xiong et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GPCR receptors are not expressed in most of the cell lines investigated in this study.
source: These receptors are not expressed in most of the cell lines investigated here, and do not influence the hyperacetylation phenotype when they are (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Butyrate is likely capable of inducing HDAC inhibition in the colon, where extracellular concentrations of butyrate are often >10 mM.
source: Butyrate especially is likely capable of inducing HDAC inhibition in the colon, where extracellular concentrations of butyrate are often >10 mM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the IC50 values and known physiological concentrations.

claim: Butyrate leads to higher levels of histone acetylation than propionate at the 1 mM treatment concentration, but not at the 100 µM treatment concentration.
source: In fact, this may be the reason that butyrate leads to higher levels of histone acetylation than propionate at the 1 mM treatment concentration (Figure 1), but not at the 100 µM treatment concentration (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the data in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: Butyrate is the subject of over 100 active clinical trials.
source: This is especially important in the case of butyrate, which is the subject of over 100 active clinical trials.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about current clinical research.

claim: There is evidence that low SCFA concentrations can have widely different physiological effects while still increasing histone acetylation.
source: In fact, there is already evidence that low SCFA concentrations can have widely different physiological effects while still increasing histone acetylation (Biermann et al., 2011; Donohoe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Many studies use high doses of SCFAs (5–30 mM), even in regions of the body where physiological concentrations should be thousands of times lower.
source: Many studies use high doses of SCFAs (5–30 mM), even in regions of the body where physiological concentrations should be thousands of times lower.
evidence: This is a statement about current research practices.

claim: High doses of SCFAs may not be necessary to induce hyperacetylation and could in fact obscure biologically relevant pathways.
source: It is possible that these doses are not necessary to induce hyperacetylation and could in fact obscure biologically relevant pathways.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.
